title: Haskell
body:
The language this course is taught in, and the reason the course is not a survey. Haskell is
[[Lambda Calculus]] with names, a type system, and a compiler: the three constructs are still
variable, abstraction, and application, and everything else in the language is sugar over
them or a checking discipline layered on top.

Three properties, and each one costs you something real:

| Property | What it means | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure** | functions are [[Pure Function\|mathematical functions]]; no assignment, no side effects | effects need [[Monadic IO]] to happen at all |
| **Lazy** | nothing is evaluated until demanded, see [[Lazy Evaluation]] | you lose the ability to predict *when* anything runs, and space leaks become possible |
| **Statically typed** | every expression has a type known before the program runs, see [[Static Typing]] | the compiler rejects programs that would have worked |

Most languages have one of these. Haskell is the mainstream language that took all three at
once, and the course's whole argument is that they reinforce each other: purity is what makes
laziness safe (if evaluation order cannot be observed, the compiler may choose it), and the
type system is what makes purity enforceable rather than a convention.

## What it looks like

```haskell
double :: Int -> Int          -- a type signature, usually optional (Type Inference)
double x = x * 2

sumTo :: Int -> Int           -- no loop exists; Recursion is the only repetition
sumTo 0 = 0                   -- base case, by pattern matching
sumTo n = n + sumTo (n - 1)   -- shrinking argument

evens = [x | x <- [1..], even x]   -- List Comprehension over an infinite list
```

`evens` is infinite and the program still terminates, because `take 5 evens` only ever demands
five elements. That is [[Lazy Evaluation]] in one line, and it is impossible in [[C]].

Note what is missing: no `for`, no `while`, no assignment. `x = x + 1` is not an increment, it
is an equation with no solution. Names bind once, which is [[Immutability]] at the language
level rather than as a style guide.

## Against the languages already in the degree

| | [[C]] | [[Java]] | [[JavaScript]] | Haskell |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Types checked | compile time, weakly | compile time | run time | compile time, strongly |
| Types written | always | always | never | rarely ([[Type Inference]]) |
| Mutation | everywhere | inside objects | everywhere | nowhere |
| Repetition | loops | loops | loops | [[Recursion Schemes\|recursion]] |
| Polymorphism | none | subtype, see [[Polymorphism]] | duck typing | [[Parametric Polymorphism]] and [[Type Class]] |
| Effects | anywhere | anywhere | anywhere | only in `IO` |

[[C]]'s "compile time, weakly" is the contrast worth holding on to: C checks types and then
lets you [[Type casting\|cast]] around the check, so its static typing is advisory. Haskell has
no cast. That is what makes "static" mean more than "not Python".

## Core Facts to Know

- Haskell is pure, lazy, and statically typed, all three at once.
- It is [[Lambda Calculus]] with names, types, and a compiler.
- There is no assignment and no loop; `=` is definition, not mutation.
- Functions are defined by equations, usually several, selected by pattern matching.
- Type signatures are optional because of [[Type Inference]], and written anyway as documentation.
- Purity is what makes [[Lazy Evaluation]] safe: unobservable evaluation order can be chosen freely.
- Effects are values of type `IO a` and cannot happen anywhere else. See [[Monadic IO]].
- Every function takes exactly one argument; `f x y` is `(f x) y`. See [[Partial Application]].
